utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-29/1-PT, the Prosecutor versus Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And may we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour -- Your Honours. Good afternoon. Appearing for the Prosecution, Mr. Stefan Waespi, on my left; Ms. Carolyn Edgerton; Mr. John Docherty; our case manager, Ms. Jasmina Bosnjakovic; and my name is Alex Whiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'm Branislav Tapuskovic, attorney-at-law from Belgrade here on behalf of Mr. Milosevic. Branislava Isailovic attorney-at-law from Paris is my co- counsel, and Ruzica Jovanovic is our legal assistant. That's our team, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic. And may I inquire whether the accused can hear the proceedings in a language that he understands.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please know that the accused answered affirmatively.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. It was a slip of the tongue on my part. I said that I was here on Slobodan Milosevic, whereas I really am here on behalf of Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Shades of the past, Mr. Tapuskovic. I must let you know that the Bench that will be conducting this trial is composed of Judge Antoine Mindua on my right, and Judge Frederik Harhoff on my left. This is a pre-trial conference, and its purpose is the usual one of considering and deciding on matters that will ensure the smooth running of the trial. To that end, there are a number of matters that I would like to discuss this afternoon, and you have been apprised of them. I must first mention that the Trial Chamber has rendered its decisions on the indictment on the dates for the start of the trial and on the 65 ter exhibit and witness list. I turn next to the question of the time available for the Prosecution case. In exercise of its powers under Rule 73 bis, the Trial Chamber had earlier fixed the time of 212 hours for the presentation of the Prosecution case. The Prosecution, in its motion for variation of the witness list, clarified that their time related to the full examination of a witness. The Chamber has been informed that a motion pursuant to Rule 92 bis will be filed in due course, and we understand that this motion will cover most or all of the 92 bis witnesses. And I am to say, Mr. Whiting, that the sooner this is filed the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, we -- depending on what time we get out of court today we're hoping to be able to file it today. If it's later, then certainly by tomorrow morning, and it will cover many, though not all, of the 92 bis witnesses, but certainly many of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How many will it not cover?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I was hoping you would ask me how many would it cover that's easier to answer and that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, John Docherty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: We are anticipating in putting in 92 bis for eight witnesses and 92 ter, meaning the witness will be here just for cross-examination, on a further 20 witnesses with the motion that will be filed either this afternoon or tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that's a total of 20 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- 92 bis -- 92 ter?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has reviewed the witness summaries, and in relation to that there are a few matters that I would like to raise. First, the Prosecution has indicated that two intercept operators will be heard viva voce. So witnesses are 165 and 166, so that they can authenticate and contextualise intercepts. It also intends to call one of its investigators to testify as to the authenticity, chain of custody, and methodology of the seizure of documents of the VRS. The question that arises, Mr. Tapuskovic and Mr. Whiting, is whether there is any dispute concerning the authenticity of these documents or whether the parties are in a position to agree that the requirements as to authenticity of the intercepts are met. Perhaps it is more appropriate to hear from you first, Mr. Tapuskovic, on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it will be difficult to give our position on this today. We did want to say something about these documents today, the 65 ter documents that you have admitted. There are now about 3.000 of those. I don't have the exact figure. It has been a very short time, and we were really not able to review all those 1.200 and 1.300 65 ter documents or identify them. We don't know if all of them are there, if all of them have been disclosed. We've been doing our best over the past several days to get there and to see whether all the documents have been received and whether there are still some documents that we haven't even looked at. As soon as we know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, are you then saying that you have not addressed this particular issue specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We don't know what the documents are that the Prosecution are now addressing. There has been a lot of discussion over the last few days about some confusion -- well, probably we do have those documents, but I have not been able to identify them. We have been using these documents for months, but up until this point in time we have not really been able to take it all in. As soon as tomorrow, or perhaps during the next break, we just might be able to provide an answer to that query.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm satisfied with that answer, Mr. Tapuskovic. But let me hear from Mr. Whiting on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's fair to say that there has not been significant discussion on reaching agreement with respect to the evidence for those three witnesses. We would be delighted to reach agreement, we will take it up immediately with the Defence, sit down with them, go over those witnesses and the documents that are to come in through those witnesses and seek to reach agreement so that we could drop those witnesses from our list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. I expect both parties to work immediately on this matter. Mr. Tapuskovic, I -- following on Mr. Whiting's submissions, I said that I expected both parties to work immediately on this matter and report to the Trial Chamber the results of those discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer now. My colleague has just informed me that we have already looked at those intercepts and we are not challenging their authenticity. The first time around I wasn't really able to answer, but here we have it all recorded on a list that is in the possession of my assistant. And we will not be challenging the authenticity of any of those intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Then, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It -- just so that we're careful and we know -- we're certain that we're talking about the same intercepts and that there's no confusion, I would ask just for a couple of days to consult with Defence counsel, make sure that we're all on the same page, but it sounds to me like we're going to be able to drop those two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Subject to your making sure that you're talking about the same matter, we'll wait to hear from you as quickly as possible. I turn then to a number of witnesses in respect of which the Chamber has determined that a reduction should be made. I refer first to the shelling incidents of the 26th May 1995, the 28th June 1995, and the 28th August 1995. The Prosecution intends to call five, ten, and eight witnesses respectively in respect of these witnesses. And I am to say that the Chamber sees no need to call all of these witnesses or at any rate to hear all of them viva voce. Next, the Chamber notes the Prosecution intends to call several police officers for single incidents. These incidents include the shelling, incidents of the 8th November 1994, 24th May 1995, 26th May 1995, and the 16th of June, 1995. And again, the Chamber sees no need to call all these witnesses to appear in The Hague. Next, the evidence of the witnesses W-20 and W-22 who are to testify as to the shelling incident of the 1st July 1995 appears to be cumulative. The Prosecution could call one of these witnesses to appear live or call one live and one of them under 92 bis. I turn next to two witnesses whom the Prosecution intends to call to explain the structure of the ABiH, and the Chamber sees no need to call both witnesses viva voce. One could be called live and one under 92 bis. Finally, the Chamber finds that many witnesses are to be called to testify as to the general situation in Sarajevo, including many police officers who are to testify on several sniping or shelling incidents and investigations into those incidents. The Trial Chamber sees no need to call all of them or at any rate to hear all of them live. Another example of a witness who is to testify under more general matters would be Witness 139, Avdo Vatric. He is to testify on the tram network, the power- supply to that network, and the effect of sniping on the running of trams in Sarajevo. The Trial Chamber notes that there will be several tram drivers to testify in this case, and they could possibly testify to these matters as well. In the light of those determinations, the Chamber sets the number of witnesses to be called by the Prosecution at 104 but urges the Prosecution to reconsider the number of witnesses to be called. The Chamber also determines that the Prosecution will present its case in 180 hours. This reflects the time available for full examination of the witnesses, that is examination-in-chief, cross-examination, re-examination. This decision as to the hours available may be subject to reconsideration once the Trial Chamber receives the Prosecution's application on the use of Rule 92 bis and 92 ter for presenting evidence of witnesses. Allowing some time for procedural matters and possible unexpected delays, the Prosecution case should be concluded sometime toward the end of April. I take up next disclosure matters. Rule 66, at the last 65 ter meeting, it was mentioned that the identities of all but one witness had been disclosed. The remaining disclosure under Rule 66 and 68 had been fulfilled. I am to ask whether the Defence has now been provided with the identity of every witness. The answer may come from either party but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Yes, it's correct that at the time of the 65 ter conference, there was one witness whose identity had not been disclosed to Defence, that's witness W-46, and unfortunately we still do not have the authorisation of that government, but I can assure Your Honours we are working very, very hard to get the name to the Defence. And I might add, like I did last time, that from the 65 ter description, it is obvious who the witness is, but we will get the authorisation as soon as we can, Mr. President. As you know, we were asking for leave to add 15 witnesses in early December and, Your Honours, you granted us leave to add 12 witnesses. Among these 12 witnesses, there are another three witnesses whom we are now allowed to call, and again the same problem arises that the respective government, they all belong to the same government, has not given agreement to disclose the names to the Defence. These witnesses are W-155, W-156, and W-157. And of two of these witnesses, the last two I mentioned, witness statements are still outstanding. And we have discussed, of course, Mr. President, the two witnesses W-165 and W-166, the two intercept operators who have not yet been identified, but that's an issue hopefully we can resolve by dropping them. That's the status as far as the Prosecution is concerned. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What can you do, Mr. Waespi, about expediting the securing of the government's authorisation?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think we have a record of, I don't know, half a dozen, a dozen reminders, perhaps. And what we plan is to take it up perhaps at a different level so that Defence has a chance to properly prepare. Again, it is obvious from the position of these witnesses except for one, except for W-157 who was not that senior. But the other were fairly senior and there are public documents discussed in other cases. So it's fairly clear who these witnesses are, but we aren't allowed to disclose it to the Defence before we have authorisation, but we are doing all we can, Mr. President, Your Honours, to expedite that. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let me make a correction to the determination about the time given to the Prosecution. The time remains the same, it's 180 hours, but the calculation which we have made indicates that on that basis, the Prosecution case should end early in April and not near the end of April, as I said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just briefly on that point, I just want to -- I just want to record on the record our concern about having our case reduced further. As Your Honours know, we not long ago reduced the case by a third by order of the Trial Chamber and brought it down to -- I thought in my head it was 220, but Your Honours say it was 212. And now it's been reduced further. And as Your Honours know, there -- this case may be -- it's more complicated than it may first appear in this sense that we, following along the way the Galic case was presented, we're going to be presenting specific incidents that we're going to be seeking to prove beyond a reasonable doubt and also we have to prove the campaign and some of the general witnesses Your Honour made reference to are to that end. And all I'm saying is that I'm concerned about whether we'll be able to meet that. We will of course try. We'll be taking onboard all of Your Honours' suggestions with respect to the case and calling witnesses 92 bis and 92 ter and it may be that we'll be fine and come under 180 hours. It may be that we'll be coming to Your Honours and seeking additional time, but that's something we can take up at a different time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I just say that in the Chamber's view, this is a relatively narrow case, relatively confined case which can be concluded within the time-frame set. I turn next to the question of translations and to ask Mr. Tapuskovic -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour. I would like to speak to you in French, and I shall be speaking French because I belong to the Parisian Bar Association even though I am Serb by origin. As far as disclosure of exhibits are concerned, we do have something to say, if you will allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Tapuskovic and I, we are concerned about the rights of our client, like all of you are in this courtroom, I am sure. But I would like to say that we are the most concerned as far as this issue is concerned. We were working on an indictment which is quite a different one to the one we are using now, and the indictment has been completely changed on the 31st of January, 2006. The Prosecution disclosed a number of exhibits pursuant to Article -- to Rule 65 ter, i.e., the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution, including a number of documents. And until the 12th of December, we have been working with these documents. On the 12th of December, you ruled on this issue and agreed to seeing the indictment modified. The counts in the indictment are the same, but the indictment otherwise is quite different. The numbering of the paragraphs is different, and after the 12th of December two other rulings were handed down, namely one on the 21st of December, 2006, which had to do with a 65 ter exhibit list and witness lists. To best defend our client, we would like to be given so consolidated batch of documents pursuant to Rule 65 ter (E), because our case or our case file now looks completely different since you handed down your ruling on the 12th of December, 2006, and following the two rulings that were handed down on the 21st of December, 2006. So our application runs as follows. We would like all these documents to meet the requirements of Rule 65 ter (E). That is the first application we made -- we are making --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are the provisions in that rule to which you make specific reference and on which you base your submission?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our submissions are based on Rule 65 ter (E)(ii) because we don't have the full list of witnesses the Prosecution wishes to call. And the second application which isn't quite an application per se because the Prosecution has provided a consolidated list of exhibits to meet the provisions of Rule 65 ter (E)(iii). And the Prosecution indicated to us recently that all these exhibits would be handed over to us, but that the latter would be to be vetted if they would be disclosed before the 21st of December, 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me see if I understand you. You're asking the Prosecution -- you're asking the Chamber to rule that the Prosecution a consolidated exhibit list, and the ground for that application is that the indictment has changed, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, Your Honour, because the set of documents that is with the pre-trial -- the Prosecution's pre-trial brief is no longer adopted. We don't have the right set of documents that would correspond to the indictment as it is amended now and according to the rules, and this is making our life really hard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, with the benefit of my French-speaking colleagues, I now have the point. Mr. Waespi, it seems to be the -- or, Mr. Whiting, a question of the correspondence of your exhibit list with the numbering in the new indictment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. It's not the exhibit list. The list is consolidated, I said that. Article 65 ter (E)(iii), three little I's. So here we agree. We have the consolidated list you plus the list of all the 65 ter exhibits. But as to the 65 ter (ii), two little I's, this is the witness list here, and here we did not obtain the documents that should come with all this. We don't have the entire list that would have all the elements provided for in Article 65 ter (E)(ii) and we would like to have that as soon as possible because that would really make our life easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. As I understand it, the exhibit list is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's a matter of the witness list and the 65 ter summaries for the witnesses. And if I understand correctly, the problem seems to be that because there's a new indictment with new paragraph numbering and additional paragraphs, the 65 ter summaries for the witnesses, to the extent that they refer to paragraphs in the indictment, they refer to the old indictment and not the new indictment. Of course, to the extent that they refer to counts, the counts did not change and so I don't think there's a problem there, I think it may just be with respect to paragraphs. Maybe if I could before responding see if that's correct -- if I understand correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you confirm whether that is the correct interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. So my - - yes, Mr. Whiting identified the problem correctly, that's exactly it, that's one of the problems. I believe that Article 65 ter (E)(ii), double I, I don't know how you say it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Roman 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Roman 2 is clear because it states the following: That the list of the witnesses that the Prosecution wants to call stating the name or pseudonym of each were we have that, we have four names missing, a summary of the facts that the witnesses will testify upon, we have new summaries and old summaries. Then the points of -- the reference to the counts and to the relevant paragraphs in the indictment, relevant paragraphs. And that exact is our problem. The Prosecution is here to accuse and to prove what he's pressing, and we're here to defend. That's the way it's supposed to be and not vice versa. We're supposed to answer -- we are supposed to answer to whatever is pressing -- whatever the Prosecution is pressing, but we have to know exactly what he is pressing and according to what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Whiting, then, it's (E)(ii)(c) that's at the heart of the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, Your Honour, and I appreciate the issue. We can do revised 65 ter summaries for our witnesses that address that issue so that the paragraph numbers correspond to the number indictment. We've already done that, I believe, for the new witnesses, but for the old witnesses I guess that has not been done. And I think if we do that then we will have complied fully with the rule. I might say that the new indictment, of course, was confirmed a month ago, and I would have been grateful if the Defence counsel had raised this issue, if they considered it to be an issue, earlier. We would have certainly acted upon it, but now that it's been raised, we'll act to comply with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On this specific question, Mr. Whiting, the Prosecution is to make a revision such as to meet its obligations under 65 ter (E)(ii)(c) by next week, Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, we will do that, if not sooner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And then you have some other points.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just another thing. So we asked all this on several occasions while we were corresponding with the Prosecution. So with respect to the harmonious work atmosphere, we asked this long ago but Mr. Whiting was not there unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Do you have any other points on this issue in relation to disclosure, that is?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, thank you. So another small item. I come from a different system. You're probably familiar to the French system, of course, but in France, we -- there's always an order called the closing order, the ordonnance de cloture, after which you can no longer disclose the exhibits. I know that here the Rules of Procedure and Evidence is different. There are other rules that apply. But it does take into account the different jurisdiction and different legal systems. So we did read your decision on the new list of exhibits. We had that recently. We're a bit surprised now because you received a motion by the Prosecution, and we of course got it, too, and it was asking for the admission of new exhibits; that really surprised us. Of course we will answer in writing very soon, but we're surprised because if it goes on like this, given the time that Prosecution has and the time that we will have for the cross-examination, this might lead to problems. If we continue, you know, putting forth new exhibits all the time without any deadlines, we don't know where we're going, and this is -- this is a bit of a concern for the fairness of the proceedings. So we decided to maybe suggest that you could eventually possibly write an order, deliver an order, issue an order, that would plan for a deadline. I mean, you come from the common law system and I think you are less formal and you are more practically oriented, of course, but it would be nice to make sure that we can have a way of accepting the exhibits that the Prosecution didn't have earlier and had in the last minute, but that's our motion. And of course we can write it down if you would rather have it in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would be happy to respond to such a motion in writing, but I will say this. The Rules of the Tribunal deal with this issue and this issue is dealt with in every case that appears before the Tribunal. The -- there is no rule and there's typically no order which cuts off, either in the Prosecution case or, for that matter, in the Defence case because the same issue arises time again in the Defence case, the introduction or motions to add new exhibits. The way it's dealt with under the Rules is those motions can be brought before the Trial Chamber and the issue is whether the -- whether there is prejudice to the Defence, and that is how it's dealt with. But to enter a blanket ruling at this point to cut off any possibility of such motions I think would not serve the interests of justice. And I might add that such a rule might be appropriate in domestic jurisdictions under certain types of rules where the cases are -- are more contained, where they're more manageable. It is just a fact of life that we all recognise at this Tribunal that these are - - that these are big, complicated cases. As the case moves on, issues start to become more defined were more clear that are in dispute, issues that the Trial Chamber might be more focussed on that the parties are more focussed on. And it happens -- it rises on both sides that material may arise that at one point did not appear to be relevant, important or necessary becomes more relevant. And it would be, in our view, unwise and not in the interests of reaching a just result in this case of closing any material coming before the Trial Chamber should that happen. Now, of course I recognise that there are important matters of the rights of the accused here, the rights of the accused to know the case that is against him, to have notice, and so forth. And those will -- if we seek to introduce a new exhibit, those weigh against us, I recognise that. But that will not mean, in our view, that every single case -- every single time it will be -- an exhibit should not be admitted. There will be instances, we believe, where the exhibit is important and that there is no prejudice to the Defence and so that it should come into evidence. The job of everyone here is to get to the truth of the matter fairly to the accused, and we think that that approach that has been followed in every case is the correct approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, to the extent that you have made a submission and wish a ruling on it at this stage, the Trial Chamber would deny your application. The practice of the Tribunal has invariably been not to establish a deadline for the production of exhibits. This is not to say, Mr. Whiting, that you're free or that any party is free to try to introduce an exhibit at any time during the trial. But Mr. Whiting is correct that the determination of that issue is done on the basis of prejudice, and in fact as you spoke I had intended to interrupt you and to ask you what prejudice would you suffer if given enough time to examine the exhibit. And once you are given enough time to examine the exhibit, the question of prejudice diminishes. So the ruling is that the application would be denied. I must say additionally that it matters not whether I or any other Judge comes from the common law system or the civil law system. We have an applicable law in the Tribunal which we apply, and that is applicable irrespective of the system from which a particular Judge comes. And I do wish to have that clarified, and I hope you understand that. Thank you. Now, let us proceed with the other matters --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, but we still have problems with the disclosure, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please, yes, continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Articles -- Rule 66 of the Rules of Procedure provides in its Article 1(A) --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- (ii) in a language that the accused understands, all copies of the statements of all witnesses that the Prosecution will call as well as the transcript in an application of Article 92 bis, Rule 92 ter, and Rule 92 ter quater. That's in Rule 66(A)(ii). That's a problem for us because for some new witnesses, we have not yet received all their statements according to what is written in that rule that I have just read. And it's extremely important in order to get instructions from our client and communicate with our client. I believe that that is why the Rule was written in the first place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you identify the witnesses? Can you identify the witnesses so that we can address the matter specifically with the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As of now, I can't tell you specifically because we received in a very scattered fashion a number of statements. We have a pseudonym. I don't want to unveil the identity of witnesses, of course, because we were able to guess a few of those identities, but we're not sure yet. And it's very hard for us to connect one statement that had been received in a batch of documents with the witness that is on the list because we don't have a name. We were able to double-guess it, but it's not very legal. It's a bit of guesswork.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. I see Mr. Waespi. What is the position in relation to this, because there is an entitlement under Rule 66 for the Defence to receive these documents in a language that the accused understands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, you're absolutely right and so is Ms. Isailovic. I tried to explain a few minutes ago that in relation to these four witnesses, we simply do not have yet the permission of the respective government to formally disclose these documents linked to their real identity to the Defence, and that concerns four witnesses. And we do our utmost to disclose -- to get permission to disclose and to disclose these statements. Obviously, these witnesses will not be called fairly early, but I guess towards the end of April, towards the end of our case, because it takes a lot of time, there are a lot of formalities involved with dealing with that. And as soon as -- as soon as, Mr. President, we have these statements in the original language, we disclose it. And as soon as it's translated, we disclose it as well into B/C/S. Whether you call it scattered or so, we just do it as quickly as we can. That's all I can say, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one correction. I think you meant the early part of April, because I did say that the Prosecution's case is expected to conclude the early part of April, not the latter part. Now, Ms. Isailovic, you heard what was said, and what I can say is this, that the Trial Chamber will ensure that the rights of your client are protected, that is to say that it will ensure that you receive the documents in a language which your client understands in sufficient time for you to provide a response to it in court. If the Prosecutor is unable to provide the document within a time-frame such as to ensure that you will have enough time, the Trial Chamber will not admit it, it's as simple as that, and the Prosecution must know this, that you have that obligation and the Trial Chamber will see that justice is done in this matter. Do you have other disclosure matters?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I go back now to the other disclosure matters and to ask whether the Defence has been provided with translations of all documents. Is the Defence in a position to comment on that? Have you been provided with translations of all documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we obtained a number of translations, but it's not a strict obligation on the Prosecution's side. But I think we did communicate correctly with the opposing party. But we really insisted on what is really provided for in the procedure, in the Rules. As to the translation of the documents, we did get a good number of them and we're doing our best. We understand, absolutely, the Prosecution's problems with the CLSS, you know, the translation office is -- has to translate a huge amount of exhibits. We believe it's a lot of work and I'm sure we'll have to face exactly the same problem when we will be having to translate our own exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I turn next to agreed facts and adjudicated facts. In May of 2006, the Prosecution made a proposal for list of potentially nondisputed facts, and this matter has been discussed at two Status Conferences. On the 2nd of November, last year, the Defence said that it had not yet replied to the proposal of the Prosecution. The Defence also said that in its pre-trial brief, it accepts some of the suggested agreed facts. At the previous 65 ter meeting, the parties indicated that they would continue their negotiations that very afternoon. And so the question I have is: What progress has been made in the negotiations on agreed facts? Mr. Whiting first.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, on this matter I'm going to defer to Mr. Docherty. It's -- he's been handling it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. The Court set forth the history of this issue quite accurately. We sent a letter to our opposing counsel on the 9th of May of the past year, 2006. The Defence has indicated on a couple of occasions that they are handicapped in responding to our overture because of needing translations of 424 documents, which, although not strictly called for by the Rules, the Prosecution nevertheless undertook to translate in view of their identification by the Defence as particularly important. And I'm sorry to say that the translation of those 424 documents became a story unto itself which continues today. We have made significant progress in getting down the 424 documents. I am informed that another batch of translations came in yesterday or perhaps just this morning, and that as soon as we have time to give them a brief check, those will be disclosed to the Defence. So we are hopeful that in the near future, and I understand of course that "in the near future" is a vague term, but this is not something entirely within the Prosecution's control, the Defence will have the information that it requires in order to respond to the Prosecution's request that we agreed to approximately 360 facts which otherwise might need to be the subject of court time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do I understand then that of the 424 documents, some have in fact been translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: A number have in fact been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: A number. And have those been passed over to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Other than the ones I referred to that have just been received last night, yes, they have been disclosed. And the other ones from last night I referred to will be disclosed today, depending on what time court rises today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. May I hear from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the speaker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. These are very important questions that we are facing at this moment. This list, or rather, this proposal that the Prosecutor gave us in relation to facts on which we are supposed to agree in order to facilitate your work primarily, and as well as the work of all of the participants in the trial, that is to say the Prosecution and the Defence, involves very complex subject matter in view of the number of facts proffered. It is over 300 facts, and it required a great amount of time so we had to work on this a great deal in order to reach the status of agreed facts. Now, what were the problems? As we were working on these matters -- well, the dates aren't important now -- it was signaled that there would be a change in the indictment, and in that situation the indictment came in in a completely new form in terms of paragraphs, where some things were explained very well, the Defence for the first time now has an indictment in relation to which it can have a relationship of its own in the full sense of the word. Now we are in a situation before such a new indictment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Tapuskovic please not touch the microphone with his paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you're being asked not to touch the microphone with your paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, I think that it is indispensable for the Prosecution, at this point in time, to react to this new indictment and to give us facts that we can discuss. Although it may seem unacceptable or unconvincing, to a great extent these fundamental explanations from the indictment that have to do with the paragraphs that pertain to everything but the matters related to the indictment itself, because nothing has changed there, so in this situation until we get a new offer in that sense, we really could not do anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, are you saying that this exercise, this whole exercise, needs to be restarted because the indictment has been changed so fundamentally and the Prosecution must resubmit a new offer?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Perhaps we haven't understood each other right. But what I was talking about were 65 ter (H) matters. I was not talking about 94, Rule 94. I was talking about facts that we were supposed to agree upon, hopefully agreed facts, adjudicated facts. That is what I spoke of, actually, and in view of the new indictment, I believe it is indispensable for the Prosecution to make a new offer to us on the basis of which we could have further discussions, because, please, indeed it is in our interest as well to not discuss certain matters that we can agree upon beforehand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me hear from -- is it Mr. Whiting or Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, Your Honour. I am at a bit of a loss, I confess, as to how to respond to that undertaking by Mr. Tapuskovic. It appears that there is a linkage between the amendment of the indictment and some infirmity in the list of proposed agreed facts which has been furnished to the Defence. And I confess - and perhaps I'm missing something - that I can't identify what that infirmity is. I have the list of proposed agreed facts in front of me and I am not clear that there is any linkage between these proposed agreed facts and the format of the indictment. As I say, perhaps I'm missing something. I stand ready to be educated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, it is also my understanding that the whole purpose of the exercise that we went through in reducing the indictment, reducing the crime sites and the consequential amendment was to clarify matters but you're saying in a sense they appear to have made matters more difficult for you. Could you clarify specifically how or why you would require the Prosecution to re-submit on this issue. Where is the ambiguity?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is no ambiguity, but the indictment has been amended. For the most part, as for the paragraphs in the indictment that go on to explain very important things related to the charges themselves, this indictment is a new and better one, a clearer one, and tells us more about the key issues, something that we didn't see in the original indictment. The situation being what it is, I don't think I should tire you pointing out the differences that do exist because there are differences and there are quite many of those. Given what the situation is, given all the explanations, and given the way the new indictment is based, we must be given a new offer, as it were, a new opportunity in terms of these agreed facts. Even today, I believe, we can agree on a number of facts, I don't think that's a problem at all, maybe even a considerable number of facts. But as far as essential facts are concerned that regard the very charges raised against Dragomir Milosevic, such as they're explained in this new indictment, indeed what was tabled, what was offered back in May 2006 was simply inadequate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think the best solution for this is for the parties to get together and work on the agreed facts. I think when you meet, Mr. Docherty, you will perhaps have a better understanding of what the problem is, and then you should both report to the Chamber by next week Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think we're quite done talking about the 94 (B), Rule 94 (B) facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, if you have other matters to raise, raise them, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as that is concerned, Your Honours, I had several things to say, important things. Needless to say, we studied carefully the position of the OTP in relation to this, and one thing I can say is that I absolutely agree with the position put forward by the OTP in their motion about the formal acknowledgement of the adjudicated facts under Rule 94 -- 94 (B). However, I'm greatly gladdened, if I may put it that way, by the OTP's position expressed in that motion, where they said explicitly, accordingly the adjudicated facts do not confirm the criminal liability of the accused. I'm aware of that and this is something that was at work in many of the previous trials before this Tribunal. It is the issue of judicial economy. I have heard the OTP emphasis when they address this issue that a balance must be had between judicial economy and the rights of the accused and the right to a fair trial on the other. It is my concern now that if these positions are not taken into account, those expressed in the OTP motion and the relevant reflections addressed in that motion, that just for the sake of judicial economy this trial may prove not to be entirely fair. I am, on the other hand, convinced that the Trial Chamber will do everything within their power, despite the Galic sentence, the Galic judgement, to, if necessary, deal with the issues that were raised in that trial and for those principles to be fully upheld. I understand the need to do everything in order to comply with the need for judicial economy and to save our resources. I am, however, convinced that the Trial Chamber will definitely take into account all of the issues that I now just pointed out. I do, of course, believe that the OTP motion is fully justified the way it's been put to us and there's nothing more to say about that. Rule 94 is crystal clear. These issues must be formally acknowledged. I do have one thing to say about that, though, and this may be food for thought. This is about agreed facts. The agreed facts under 54 and 55 in the OTP document. This is the term "campaign" and "sniping," these are two terms. In my understanding, these should not be agreed facts or unchallenged facts. This is just a position, it's how they qualified this, and I'm sure that the Trial Chamber will ponder this. I do not think, however, at this point in time we can take that to be an agreed fact and use it in a different case, something that was pondered and ruled upon by this Chamber. So that's what I think about these two specific facts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the Chamber will overlook the fact that you're out of time because your deadline expired on the 5th of January, that's the deadline for responding. This is a very important matter. It raises legal issues that need to be considered carefully. So you must file a written response, and you are to file that response within a week, by next week, Friday. I turn next to expert witnesses. The Prosecution has notified the Chamber and the parties that it intends to call five expert witnesses, but we have only received the report of one expert. Is it Mr. Docherty to explain what the position is in relation to -- to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I can -- what I can do is take them by witness number in order and simply apprise the Chamber and the Defence of the status of the various reports, if that's the best way to proceed. Witness number 9 is an expert on ballistics or artillery and mortars. A first draft report has been received and disclosed to the Defence, a second draft has been received last week. It is being reviewed by the Prosecution and upon conclusion of that review which will be finished shortly. The report will then be disclosed to the Defence. Witness number 128 is an expert on sniping. This expert has appeared before this Tribunal before in the Prlic case. He did a report relating to sniping incidents in the city of Mostar. That report, even though it doesn't relate to Sarajevo, was disclosed to the Defence because the report which this expert will do in our case is going to be very similar in methodology and technique to the Mostar case. A draft of this expert's report has been received. It is being revised. I anticipate disclosing the expert sniping report within one week. Witness number 3, a military and document analysis expert, that report is done. It will be disclosed to the Defence early next week after proofreading and final vetting by the Prosecution. And as the Court notes, the report of witness number 8 has been completed and disclosed and submitted for translation. There are two experts, Witnesses 15 and 132 whose reports are not in -- as near completion as those which I have just talked about. Witness number 15 is an expert on air bombs, a type of weapon which we anticipate hearing something about during this trial. We are awaiting that report. The witness number 15 has explained to us that the report is a bit lengthy which is why it is taking some time. And witness number 132 is an expert on demographics who was examining death record, hospital records, and so forth related to the indictment period in Sarajevo. And that expert is working through those databases, but as of yesterday was unable to give the Prosecution a deadline by which that report would be received. Let me assure the Court and the Defence, however, that what Your Honour, Mr. President, said a little while ago is something that is neither surprising nor troubling to us, which is that of course we cannot make use of evidence as to which proper notice has not been received by the Defence. We understand that, and we will, therefore, keep pressing to get these expert reports done. We anticipate that in the end there will be no problems, and that all of these reports will be timely completed, timely translated, timely submitted. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Docherty. Anything from the Defence on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I can say is what is precisely envisaged in Rule 94 bis as far as experts are concerned. It was on the 5th of January that we received the expert report of W-8, expert W- 8. That was on the 5th of January, and we are adamant that the 30-day deadline should be complied with from the day we received the expert report to the day we are supposed to address the issue, unless of course the Chamber rules otherwise, then we shall comply. And that is just about all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber is not ruling otherwise, Mr. Tapuskovic. I turn next to the outstanding motions. There is a motion for admission of documentary evidence with confidential annexes, and that was filed on the 20th of December. The Defence has not yet responded, but the deadline expired on the 8th of January, 2007, and the Chamber intends to give its decision on this motion shortly. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have not noticed anything. We believe that we can accept this. We wrote nothing. We take note of the existence of these documents, and they can be used in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic. There is a Prosecution notice pursuant to Rule 94 bis, disclosure of expert report of Robert Donia filed on the 5th of January, 2007. The deadline for the Defence response expires on the 5th of February, and the Chamber will issue its decision in due course. There's a Prosecution motion for the admission of a witness written statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter with a confidential annex filed on the 5th of January. Now, the deadline for the Defence response is Friday, the 19 of January, but, Mr. Whiting, this witness is scheduled to testify in the week of the 15th. So the question is this: The Defence has until the 19th, next week, Friday. If the Defence is able to file its response by Monday, the 15th, we could proceed, you know. If not, the Prosecution must arrange for this witness to testify at a later stage and ensure that there is a witness available to take his place. So the first question then, Mr. Tapuskovic, is whether the Defence would be able to file its response by Monday, the 15th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can tell you right away, Your Honours, that we accept for that witness to appear as the first witness in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. There is another witness that gives rise to the same problem. This is the motion for the admission of witness transcripts pursuant to Rule 92 ter filed on the 9th January, and the Defence deadline for response is the 23rd of January, but this witness is going to be heard on the 15th of January. And here again, if the Defence is able to file its response by the 12th of January, we could proceed. If not, then the Prosecution must ensure that there is another witness available to take his place. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would need very short time, Your Honour. Maybe after the break we're able to answer that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is my understanding accurate? Both witnesses will be facing the Chamber on the 15th, that is Monday; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, this is the first witness, actually, the one that we're dealing with now is the first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My understanding was there were two requests. I granted my request to one of the requests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other request concerning the other witness due to appear before the Chamber that same week but not on that same day. That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness that we're dealing with now, that is the witness transcript pursuant to Rule 92 ter, in respect of that witness you have until the 23rd of January. That witness, I understand, is the first witness due to testify. So the question that I asked - and I'm not putting any pressure on you at all because you have until the 23rd - the matter really rests with the Prosecution. If you are not in a position to file your response by the 12th of January, then the Prosecution must find another witness because we will not tolerate any breakdown. What is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we shall be providing a response very soon, as soon as tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we have to take a break because we have been here for an hour and a half. We break for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have a few more matters to conclude. Still dealing with outstanding motions, there's a Prosecution motion for protective measures filed on the 9th of January, and the Defence is to respond by the 23rd of January. So the Trial Chamber will issue its decision on this motion in due course. Scheduling of witnesses. The parties are to provide a list of witnesses every Thursday with the names of the witnesses they expect to call the following week. The Prosecution will supplement that list with all known prior statements of the witness that are relevant to the proceedings. I hope that is clear. I deal next with the presentation of documents -- yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, just to be absolutely clear. The -- the statements -- does the Trial Chamber also want the statements or are you contemplating that these statements are provided just to the Defence? It's been different practice in different cases, so I just wasn't clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The intention is that the statements will also be provided to the Chamber. The parties are to provide a list of exhibits they intend to use in court during examination-in-chief and cross-examination, and these lists are to be available to the opposing party, the Registry, and the Chambers no later than 48 hours in advance. But when the total number of pages exceed 100, the list of documents must be provided no later than 72 hours prior to the testimony of the witness. And I hope that is understood. Now, are there any other matters to be raised by the parties? Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one that I think of and Mr. Waespi apparently has something else that he would like to raise. Just, again, to be clear with respect to the exhibits. I take it that those can be provided to the opposing party, Registry, and Chambers through the e- court, that is the Chamber does not require hard copies of those exhibits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I confirmed that they may be provided by e-court. Is there a matter that the Defence wishes to raise in relation to this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether I understood this right, but every Thursday the schedule for the next week will be set. Is that right? That was my understanding of it. That means that some of these witnesses that we would be directed to deal with on a particular Thursday could be called already on the next Monday. That is too short a period of time. I think that a bit more time is needed for disclosing the witnesses that are to appear during the following week. This is too short a period of time. Of course, that is my opinion and of course we will abide by your ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I certainly appreciate what Mr. Tapuskovic is saying and understand. It actually had been our intention to try to give at least a week's notice -- at least a week's notice, if not more, if not two week's notice for witnesses. So a witness who is called on a Monday will be noticed to the Defence the previous Monday is our goal, our aim. And that is what we will try to endeavour to do. I had understood Your Honour's Thursday deadline to be the kind of final list and the list that goes to the Chamber, but between ourselves, we will be giving more advanced notice so they will have a chance to prepare. And certainly if there is an instance where they believe they have not received enough notice, that is something they can raise with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll consider this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered this matter and has determined that the list of witnesses should be provided at least one week prior to the testimony. And where the Prosecution provides that list before that time, then it should also at that time notify the Chamber as well. There was another matter that you wished to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, I think we've resolved it. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have come to a point in time when I can raise any issue. Is that right, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Having heard the submissions, we'll hear you in private session and the previous submissions will be redacted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no matters to raise in relation to all these issues that you have mentioned. My health is under consideration. I'm undergoing certain examinations, medical examinations, they are in progress. I don't know the results yet. So much for that. Everything else is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milosevic. In that event, then, we'll adjourn until tomorrow when the trial will commence with the Prosecution's opening statement at 2.15 in this courtroom. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 11th day of January, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.27 p.m.,
